translationRepairs: He was transferred from Palace Attendant to Left Assistant Commandant.
He was transferred from Cadet of the Heir Apparent's Household to Left Assistant Commandant.
中庶子 is a post in the heir apparent's household, not 侍中 (Palace Attendant), which the chapter uses separately for Xu Xiang.

Sun Quan again roared with laughter.
權又大噱 says Sun Quan again laughed heartily; "until he cried" is an invention and "again" (又) is omitted.
The first holder had been Palace Attendant Xu Xiang; when Xu died, Ke was slated to succeed him.
The first holder had been Palace Attendant and Major-General Xu Xiang; when Xu died, Ke was slated to succeed him.
The idiomatic omits Xu Xiang's second office 偏將軍 (Major-General).
He asked to colonize the fields at Wan Mouth in Lujiang, then strike Shu with a flying column, scoop up the people, and retire before Wei could react.
He asked to colonize the fields at Wan Mouth in Lujiang, then raid Shu County with light troops, seize its people by surprise, and return.
舒 is Shu County in Lujiang, not the state of Shu (蜀); "before Wei could react" is not in the Chinese.

As for Zizhang, Zilu, Zigong, and the rest of the seventy—men next only to the Sage—they still each had his flaw; the Master faulted You for rashness and Xi for refusing orders—how much more must lesser men show gaps?

As for Zizhang, Zilu, Zigong, and the rest of the seventy—men next only to the Sage—they still each had his flaw; Shi (Zizhang) was one-sided, You (Zilu) coarse, and Ci (Zigong) did not accept his lot—how much more must lesser men show gaps?
師闢由喭，賜不受命 names the three disciples by personal name (師 Zizhang, 由 Zilu, 賜 Zigong); 師 is not "the Master" and there is no "Xi".
Confucius never dismissed Gongxi Zihua for lacking polish; he prized gifts and forgave faults.
Confucius did not spurn these disciples for their shortcomings but drew them close as friends, never discarding a man's strengths because of his weaknesses.
數予 (for 數子, "these several men") refers back to the disciples just named; Gongxi Zihua is not mentioned in the Chinese.
So Zhang Er and Chen Yu drew steel; Xiao Wangzhi and Zhu Bo parted—for no deeper cause than this.
So Zhang Er and Chen Yu drew steel; Xiao Yu and Zhu Bo parted—for no deeper cause than this.
蕭、朱 who "did not keep their friendship to the end" are Xiao Yu and Zhu Bo of Han, as the literal translation has it, not Xiao Wangzhi.
Later Han watched Prince Liu Dan of Yan intrigue with Princess Gai until revolt boiled—the Shangguan crisis all over again; in such an hour who could rest easy?
In the Han of recent memory Prince Liu Dan of Yan intrigued with Princess Gai until the Shangguan revolt broke out; in such an hour who could rest easy?
近漢 means the Han of recent times; the Yan-Gai-Shangguan affair belongs to Western Han under Emperor Zhao, not Later Han, and it was the event itself, not a repeat of it.

Your sector meshes with the enemy's lines like dogs' teeth—you must drill arms, rouse men, watch harder than common duty, pledge ten thousand deaths for one life of service, pay the dynasty, honor the clan.
與賊犬牙相錯 describes interlocking lines; the idiomatic is ungrammatical.
He killed informers, shelved spies, forgave arrears, lifted tolls—the reign ran on mercy and the realm sang.
He abolished surveillance, idled the investigating officials, forgave arrears, lifted tolls—the reign ran on mercy and the realm sang.
罷視聽，息校官 abolishes surveillance and idles investigators; nobody was killed.
December’s win went to his head; come spring he hungered for another campaign.
The twelfth-month victory went to his head; come spring he hungered for another campaign.
十二月 is the twelfth lunar month, not the Gregorian December.
Wu and Shu together are not half that footprint.
Compared with the six states of old, Wu and Shu together are not half their size.
以吳與蜀比古穴國(=六國)，不能半之 compares Wu and Shu with the ancient six states; the idiomatic drops the comparison.
He mobilized anew—eyes on Huangzhou and Xuzhou.
He mobilized anew—eyes on Qing and Xu provinces.
責、徐 is a graphic error for 青、徐 (Qing and Xu provinces); there is no "Huangzhou" here.

Sun Jun, exploiting the hatred, accused Ke of plotting a coup, conspired with Sun Liang, and baited Ke with a banquet.
構恪欲為變，與亮謀 means Sun Jun framed Ke as plotting revolt and conspired with (Sun) Liang; the idiomatic obscures who was accused.

Zhang Yue and Zhu En slipped a note: “Today’s arrangements are unusual—we suspect another purpose.”
今日張設非常，疑有他故 speaks of today's arrangements and a suspected plot, not "tonight".
Ke quoted Confucius—“Twice is enough”—“Ten times insults my wit.”
Ke replied, “Of old Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting, and the Master said, ‘Twice will do.’ Now you bid me think ten times—you are declaring me a dunce.”
The idiomatic omits Ji Wenzi (季文子三思而後行), on whom the Master's remark comments.
He read calm as settled strategy—the gentleman fears, then wins by plotting.
Lai Min meant that Fei Yi's strategy was settled within though he showed no worry; yet Changning held that a gentleman approaches affairs with apprehension and succeeds by careful planning.
況長寧以為… attributes the maxim to Changning, who is omitted in the idiomatic.

Having formerly heard Changning's critique of Wenwei (Fei Yi) and now seeing Yuansun's (Zhuge Ke's) rebuff of Marquis Lü, Yu Xi records the two parallel cases together as a lasting warning to posterity.〉
The idiomatic drops the named parties 長寧, 文偉 (Fei Yi), 元遜 and 呂侯.

Jian crossed the Yangzi meaning to flee north to Wei, but after thousands of li the pursuers caught him.
為追兵所逮: he was caught by the (Wu) pursuers, not by Wei; 數千里 is thousands of li.

The Palace Attendant, General Who Guards the Martial, Marquis of Duxiang—both bore the late emperor’s testamentary edict; seeing Ke’s wicked cruelty swell day by day, fearing he would shake the cosmos and overturn altars of soil and grain, they roused awesome wrath, essence piercing the azure sky, counsel anticipating gods, wit and daring surpassing Jing Ke and Nie Zheng; gripping naked blades they struck Ke’s head in the hall—merit exceeding the Marquis of Zhuxu, deeds outdoing the Marquis of Dongmou.

Gaozu buried enemies with honor—so should Wu.

The idiomatic omits the named examples 項籍 and 韓信, and "so should Wu" is not in the source.

子嘿 (Gu Tan) and 子直 (Gu Cheng) were brothers, not cousins, and it was Nie You who gained fame (由是知名).
Wei’s boy emperor drools while regents feud—ripe rot within.

曹勞(芳)暗劣，而政在私門 says Cao Fang is dim and power is in private hands; "boy emperor drools" and "regents feud" are invented.

Teng Yin, as father-in-law of Zhuge Ke's son Song, offered to resign.

In the second year Wei's Guanqiu Jian and Wen Qin rebelled with their troops and fought the Wei army at Lejia; Sun Jun led Lü Ju and Liu Zan to raid Shouchun, but when Wen Qin was defeated and came over, the army returned.
The idiomatic drops that Jian and Qin were Wei rebels fighting Wei forces and that Qin surrendered (敗降).

The plot leaked; Sun Yi and others killed themselves, and several tens died, Princess Lu Yu among them.
儀等自殺 applies suicide to Sun Yi and his associates; the several tens who died, including Princess Luyu, are not all suicides.
Year after, Qin talked Jun into another thrust—hosts left Jiangdu for Qing-Xu.

The next year Wen Qin persuaded Sun Jun to attack Wei; Jun sent Qin with Lü Ju, General of Chariots and Cavalry Liu Zuan, General Who Guards the South Zhu Yi and General of the Van Tang Zi from Jiangdu into the Huai and Si to strike at Qing and Xu.

Lin bottled Ju at Jiangdu while envoys pressured Yin; Yin held Hua Rong hostage, armed his household, and denounced Lin.

Hearing this, Lin sent his elder cousin Sun Lü with troops to intercept Ju at Jiangdu, had palace envoys order Wen Qin, Liu Zuan, Tang Zi and others to attack Ju, and sent Palace Attendant and General of the Left Hua Rong and Deputy of the Secretariat Ding Yan to tell Yin to seize Ju and to leave quickly. Yin, judging that disaster had reached him, detained Hua Rong and Ding Yan, armed his troops for self-defence, summoned Army Controller Yang Chong and General Sun Zi, declared that Lin was in revolt, and forced Hua Rong and the others to write letters denouncing Lin.
The idiomatic omits the named participants 慮, 文欽, 劉纂, 唐諮, 丁晏, 揚崇 and 孫諮.
〈The Wenshi zhuan says: Hua Rong, courtesy name Derui, was from Jiangdu in Guangling.
文士傳 is a book title (Wenshi zhuan), not "literary tradition"; the idiomatic also drops Guangling.
Ancestors fled war to Shanyin hills.
His grandfather fled the turmoil and settled below Mount Rui in Shanyin.
祖父 is his grandfather, not "ancestors".
Teng Yin's expression did not change; he talked and laughed as usual.
顏色不變，談笑若常 describes composure during the siege, not facing death smiling.
He told his men Ju was close—hold the line—but Ju never came.
Finding it hard to raise troops against the palace, he instructed his retainers that Marquis Lü was on the road nearby, so they all fought to the death for Yin and none scattered.
The idiomatic omits that his men all fought to the death without scattering (皆為胤盡死，無離散者).
Sun Lin stormed in—slaughtered Yin’s clan to the third degree.
Sun Lin's troops converged, killed Yin and several tens of his officers, and exterminated Yin's kin to the third degree.
The idiomatic omits the killing of Teng Yin himself and of several tens of officers.
Sun Lü had backed Ke—Jun raised him to right general and inner-court fixer.

Earlier, Jun's younger cousin Sun Lü had taken part in the plot against Zhuge Ke; Jun favored him, raising him to General of the Right and Commander of the Wunan guard, with insignia and canopy, in charge of the affairs of the nine palaces.
與諸葛恪之謀 means he joined the plot against Ke, not that he backed Ke; 無難督 is a guard command, not an "inner-court fixer".
Wu sent thirty thousand under Wen Qin and Quan brothers.
Wu sent Wen Qin, Tang Zi, Quan Duan, Quan Yi, and others, thirty thousand men, to relieve him.
The idiomatic names only Wen Qin and Quan brothers, omitting Tang Zi and calling the Quan men brothers, which the Chinese does not say.
Qin and the others broke through the siege.
欽等 names Qin and his column; the idiomatic replaces them with an unnamed relief column.
Zhu Yi camped at Ancheng to back Qin.
Zhu Yi led thirty thousand men to camp at Anfeng and support Wen Qin.
安豐城 is Anfeng, not Ancheng.
Sun Lin stacked fifty thousand under Zhu Yi at Huoli—supplies at Dulü.
Lin then raised a large force and camped at Huoli. He again sent Yi with generals Ding Feng, Li Fei, and others, fifty thousand men, to attack Wei, leaving the baggage at Dulü.
The idiomatic puts the fifty thousand under Zhu Yi at Huoli and drops Ding Feng and Li Fei. The Chinese has Lin encamped at Huoli and Yi leading the attack.
Wu blamed Lin for killing Zhu Yi and losing Dan.
Lin had failed to extricate Dan, had lost his troops, and had himself killed a famous general, so everyone resented him.
莫不怨之 is general resentment. The idiomatic invents Wu as the blamer.
Ringed the capital with brothers in every gate camp.

He built a house south of the Vermilion Sparrow Bridge and sent his younger brother, General Who Inspires Awe at a Distance Ju, into the Azure Dragon guard. Younger brothers General of Martial Guards En, Major-General Gan, and Colonel of the Changshui Kai each held camps, so he could monopolize the court and secure himself.
The idiomatic omits Ju, En, Gan, and Kai and their offices.
Liang's consort, the daughter of Lin's elder female cousin, told Lin the plot.
從姊女 is the daughter of an elder female cousin, not Lin's own cousin.
Announce edict to your father—do not let your mother know—women grasp not great affairs—and Lin is cousin by hall—chance leak ruins me beyond measure.”

Announce the edict to your father, but do not let your mother know. Women do not understand great affairs, and she is Lin's paternal cousin-sister. If it leaks by chance, the harm to me will be no small thing.
同堂姊 is Quan Ji's mother, Lin's paternal cousin-sister. The idiomatic says Lin himself is the cousin.
Sun Sheng doubts chronology—smart boy would not tell wife first.
Sun Sheng says: Liang's biography calls him clever from youth, so he ought to have planned with Ji first and not let his wife know beforehand.
The comment is about whom Liang told first, not about chronology.
Pei accepts Jiang Biao leak narrative as fuller.〉
The Jiang Biao Zhuan gives the cause of the leak, and the affair is told in detail there.
The Chinese does not say that Pei accepts the account; it says the Jiang Biao Zhuan explains the leak and is detailed.

Ordered Superintendent of the Household Meng Zong announce temples deposing Liang—summoned gathered officers—“Young emperor wasteland-sick muddled mad—may not occupy great seat—carry ancestral temples—therefore announcing prior emperor’s temples—deposing him.

He had Superintendent of the Household Meng Zong announce at the temples that Liang was deposed, summoned the officers, and said, "The young emperor is dissolute, ill, and muddled. He cannot occupy the great position or uphold the ancestral temples. Having reported this to the late emperor, we depose him.
The literal renders 荒 as wasteland and muddles the report to the late emperor. 荒病昏亂 means dissolute, ill, and muddled.
〈Huan Yi was brother of Wei minister Huan Jie.
The Han Jin Chunqiu says: Yi was the younger brother of Huan Jie, Prefect of the Masters of Writing under Wei.
The idiomatic drops the book title and that Yi was the younger brother.
Jin emperor later cited Huan Yi as Wu martyr.〉
The Wu lu says: Emperor Wu of Jin asked Xue Ying about Wu's famous ministers, and Ying answered that Yi had a loyal and steadfast integrity.
The idiomatic omits Xue Ying and the Wu lu and turns Ying's reply into the Jin emperor citing Huan Yi.
Shi Zheng talked Lin into king Huima—Sun Xiu.
Shi Zheng urged Lin to summon and enthrone the Prince of Langye, Xiu, and Lin followed.
琅邪王休 is Sun Xiu, Prince of Langye. King Huima is not in the Chinese.
Charges dalliance with Liu Cheng and palace women.
He drew Liu Cheng close and delighted in beautiful women;
親近劉承，悅於美色 does not say Liu Cheng was the object of a sexual liaison.
Monstrous catalog of Liang’s alleged orgies and toy navy.

He called up women of the officials and people, kept the attractive ones in the palace, took more than three thousand younger brothers of soldiers aged eighteen and under to drill in the park day and night until great and small groaned, and ruined more than five thousand spears and halberds in the stores to make toys.
The idiomatic replaces the women, the youths, and the ruined weapons with orgies and a toy navy, which this sentence does not say.
Claims Zhu heirs murdered princess—distorts truth.
Zhu Ju was an old minister of the late emperor. His sons Xiong and Sun inherited their father's foundation and stood by loyal counsel; formerly the junior princess was killed.
The idiomatic adds a judgment that the letter distorts the truth and drops Zhu Ju, Xiong, and Sun.
Blames Liang for Zhu executions without hearing Lin’s guilt.
This was wrought by the Great Princess. The emperor never examined how it began and ended, then killed Xiong and Sun, and remonstrance was not used.
The idiomatic invents a confession of Lin's guilt, which this sentence does not state.
Chamberlain Quan Shang had received favor for generations and could not control his clansmen, and Quan Duan and others abandoned their cities and went to Wei.
The idiomatic reduces the named charges against Quan Shang and Quan Duan to an unnamed smear.
Heaven aids the sincere and settles on virtue; You and Li lost the way yet Xuan restored the house; Your Majesty inherits the great succession and deserves worthy assistants;

I have heard that Heaven's mandate is not always reliable and must settle on the virtuous. Thus Kings You and Li lost proper measure and obstructed the house until King Xuan restored it. Your Majesty's sage virtue inherits the great succession and should obtain worthy assistants;
幽、厲、and 宣 are Kings You, Li, and Xuan of Zhou. The idiomatic reads You and Li as pronouns and drops the obstruction before King Xuan's restoration.
En was made grandee secretary and guard general; Lü Ju was made general of the right.
En was made Grandee Secretary and Guard General, and Ju was made General of the Right.
據 beside En is Sun Ju. Lü Ju is a different man, named later as 呂據.
Claims he chose Xiu for virtue.
I welcomed him because Your Majesty is worthy and enlightened.
The sentence is Lin's own speech. The idiomatic replaces it with a narrator's summary.
Emperor Xiu feared Lin would bolt—showered honors and busywork to watch him.
Fearing that Lin might turn against him, he repeatedly added rewards, again granted him the favor of Palace Attendant, and shared the review of documents with Lin.
加恩 is added favor, not Sun En, and 侍中 is the office. The idiomatic's busywork is not in the Chinese. 鞏 is the received graph, likely standing for fear.
Xiu fed Lin a false informer—Lin killed him—proving brutality.
Someone reported that Lin harbored resentment, insulted the sovereign, and meant to rebel. Xiu seized the accuser, handed him to Lin, and Lin killed him.
The Chinese does not say the informer was false or that the killing proved brutality.
Lin fled toward Wuchang with elite ten thousand—throne armed him freely.

Lin therefore grew more afraid and, through Meng Zong, asked to garrison Wuchang. Xiu agreed, ordered the more than ten thousand elite central-camp troops under Lin's command to pack, and issued him all the arsenal weapons he took.
求出屯武昌 is a request Xiu granted. Lin did not simply flee, and Meng Zong is the intermediary.
Ministers called the dyke a boondoggle—Puyang Xing alone swore it would pay.
An edict called the officials to a conference. All held that the labor would be great and the fields might not be completed. Only Xing held that it could be completed.
The Chinese reports a court conference and Xing's judgment. It does not say he swore the dyke would pay.
Corvée swelled—paymasters drowned—troops died in mutiny and accident—the delta cursed Xing’s name.
They then gathered soldiers and commoners for the work. The cost of the labor could not be counted. Officers and soldiers died, some killing themselves, and the people greatly resented it.
或自賊殺 means some killed themselves. It does not say paymasters drowned or that there was a mutiny.
Raised to chancellor, he teamed with Zhang Bu—Wu groaned at crony rule.
Xing was promoted to Chancellor and worked in concert with Xiu's favorite, General of the Left Zhang Bu. Within the state, people lost hope.
張共布 is Zhang Bu with a stray graph 共. 邦內失望 is disappointment within the state.
Sun Hao bought loyalty with palace posts and a Qingzhou title.
After Hao took the throne, he added Xing as Palace Attendant and put him in charge as Governor of Qingzhou.
The Chinese states offices conferred on Xing. It does not say Hao bought loyalty.
Lin again said, "I wish to be reduced to government slaves."
Lin again said, "I wish to be reduced to a government slave."
官奴 is singular here: Lin asks that he himself be made a slave.
Chen Shou: Wu admired Ke’s brilliance, but pride and deafness to counsel ruined him—a sage regent could scarcely have controlled such ego.

The appraisal says: Zhuge Ke's talent and resource were praised by the people of the state, yet he was arrogant and stingy. The Duke of Zhou phrase in the received text is unclear; how much more so for Ke?
周公 is the Duke of Zhou, and the received 無觀 is unclear. The idiomatic adds deafness to counsel and a sage regent controlling ego.
Had Ke practiced the humility he preached to Lu Xun and Zhuge Rong, he might have died in bed.
Had he himself practiced what he wrote to Lu Xun and to his younger brother Rong, regret and blame would not have come. What ground would there have been for disaster?
The Chinese does not say he might have died in bed. 弟融 is his younger brother Rong.
Teng Yin’s rectitude could not save him once Jun turned butcher—virtue offered no armor.
Teng Yin sternly cultivated a gentleman's conduct and walked by rule and measure, yet in Sun Jun's time he still kept his high rank. That was the logic of certain danger.
The Chinese does not call Jun a butcher or say that virtue offered no armor.
Sun Jun and Sun Lin were base plotters beneath serious debate.
Jun and Lin were vicious underlings, overflowing with evil, and hardly worth extended discussion.
兇豎盈溢 is vicious underlings overflowing with evil, not only base plotters.
Puyang Xing stood at the helm yet peddled Wan Yu’s intrigue and Zhang Bu’s faction—his annihilation was earned.
Puyang Xing occupied the chief counselor's seat, but his thought did not extend to governing the state. He abetted Zhang Bu's crookedness and accepted Wan Yu's counsel. His extermination was fitting.
慮不經國 is omitted by the idiomatic. The received 宣 in 其宣矣 is taken in the sense 宜, fitting.
